query: For multicomponent high-entropy alloys in solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures, what single testable methodological intervention could overcome the inability of EAM references to represent the many atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid? Explain why it should improve reference–target phase-space overlap, predict the reduction in thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references, define the applicable composition and temperature ranges, identify supporting evidence from elemental or binary calculations, and specify a decisive free-energy benchmark that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing the standard EAM reference in thermodynamic integration with an active-learning–trained deep neural network potential will capture the diverse atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid phase in high-entropy alloys near their melting points, leading to improved reference–target phase-space overlap and a significant reduction in thermodynamic integration path mismatch compared to TOR-TILD’s traditional EAM references.
generation.material_initial_state: Multicomponent high-entropy alloys in their solid and near-melting liquid states, particularly those with refractory or high–melting-temperature compositions exhibiting significant atomic configurational diversity.
generation.intervention: Implement a deep neural network (DL) potential trained via active learning on ab initio calculations covering both solid and liquid configurations to serve as the reference for thermodynamic integration.
generation.conditions: Applicable at temperatures close to or exceeding 0.9 Tm in high-entropy alloy systems (5+ principal elements) where the liquid phase is highly disordered; especially effective for refractory alloys with melting temperatures typically greater than 2000 K.
generation.structural_mediator: The short-range order and diverse local atomic environments present in the near-melting liquid state, which are more accurately captured by the DL potential.
generation.mechanism: Active learning ensures that the DL potential is trained on a wide and representative set of atomic configurations from both solid and liquid phases. This tailored potential thus provides a reference that better overlaps with the true ab initio phase space, reducing interpolation errors and mismatches along the thermodynamic integration path relative to the EAM-based reference.
generation.predicted_outcome: An improved free-energy calculation with a reduction in thermodynamic integration path mismatch by an estimated 30–50% compared to the TOR-TILD method using traditional EAM references; accordingly, a closer agreement with independently benchmarked ab initio free-energy values.
generation.baseline: The TOR-TILD framework using conventional EAM potentials, which have been shown to inadequately represent the wide range of atomic configurations in ab initio liquid simulations near the melting point.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective in high-entropy alloys exhibiting disordered liquid structures and in composition regimes where the configurational landscape is densely sampled by the training set. It may be less effective if significant phase separation or ordering phenomena occur outside the training regime.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative reduction in integration mismatch is uncertain and will likely depend on factors such as the quality and diversity of the training data set for the DL potential. Further benchmarking against independent free-energy measurements is needed to fully establish the effect size.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform thermodynamic integration on a representative high-entropy alloy system near its melting temperature using both the standard EAM-based TOR-TILD method and the DL potential–based approach. Compare the calculated free energies with independent ab initio free-energy benchmarks.
measurements: Computed free-energy differences via thermodynamic integration
Quantitative metrics of phase-space overlap between reference and target distributions
Path integration mismatch measures (e.g., deviation lengths or error integrals)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the deep-learning potential does not achieve a statistically significant reduction (approximately 30–50% or more) in the integration path mismatch and does not produce free-energy estimates in closer agreement with independent ab initio benchmarks compared to the EAM reference, then the hypothesis should be considered falsified.

A map of single-phase high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys have exhibited unusual materials properties. The stability of equimolar single-phase solid solution of five or more elements is supposedly rare and identifying the existence of such alloys has been challenging because of the vast chemical space of possible combinations. Herein, based on high-throughput density-functional theory calculations, we construct a chemical map of single-phase equimolar high-entropy alloys by investigating over 658,000 equimolar quinary alloys through a binary regular solid-solution model. We identify 30,201 potential single-phase equimolar alloys (5% of the possible combinations) forming mainly in body-centered cubic structures. We unveil the chemistries that are likely to form high-entropy alloys, and identify the complex interplay among mixing enthalpy, intermetallics formation, and melting point that drives the formation of these solid solutions. We demonstrate the power of our method by predicting the existence of two new high-entropy alloys, i.e. the body-centered cubic AlCoMnNiV and the face-centered cubic CoFeMnNiZn, which are successfully synthesized.Subject terms: Mat

Melting simulations of high-entropy carbonitrides by deep learning potentials

Abstract: The melting temperature is a crucial property of materials that determines their potential applications in different industrial fields. In this study, we used a deep neural network potential to describe the structure of high-entropy (TiZrTaHfNb)CxN1−x carbonitrides (HECN) in both solid and liquid states. This approach allows us to predict heating and cooling temperatures depending on the nitrogen content to determine the melting temperature and analyze structure changes from atomistic point of view. A steady increase in nitrogen content leads to increasing melting temperature, with a maximum approaching for 25% of nitrogen in the HECN. A careful analysis of pair correlations, together with calculations of entropy in the considered liquid phases of HECNs allows us to explain the origin of the nonlinear enhancement of the melting temperature with increasing nitrogen content. The maximum melting temperature of 3580 ± 30 K belongs to (TiZrTaHfNb)C0.75N0.25 composition.
